claims: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a natural, irregular climate cycle.
The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) involves alternating warm (El Niño) and cold (La Niña) ocean surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific.
The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is accompanied by shifts in atmospheric pressure.
ENSO typically impacts global weather patterns every two to seven years.
El Niño, La Niña, and Neutral.
El Niño is the warm phase with weakened trade winds.
La Niña is the cold phase with strong trade winds.
Changes in the Pacific Ocean temperatures affect the atmosphere (wind/pressure).
The atmosphere in turn changes ocean temperatures.
El Niño often brings wetter conditions to the southern U.S.
El Niño often brings drier weather to Australia and Southeast Asia.
La Niña typically causes the reverse.
Cooler La Niña waters can increase fish populations.
Warmer El Niño waters can reduce Atlantic hurricane activity.
Humanity cannot control the ENSO cycle.
Institutions like NOAA use the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) to predict these events.
Institutions like NOAA provide early warnings to mitigate impacts, particularly for agriculture.
